title: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
summary: Run a security programme as a leader: maturity and roadmaps, budgets and prioritisation, metrics, board reporting, team design and hiring, crisis leadership, disclosure rules and the CISO liability cases.
outcomes: Explain what a CISO is accountable for and compare reporting lines by independence and information flow
Compute C2M2 maturity levels and turn target gaps into a dependency-ordered roadmap
Build a security budget and rank initiatives by expected loss removed per dollar
Choose metrics that drive decisions and detect when a target has corrupted a measure
Size round-the-clock coverage and design hiring around methods that predict performance
Describe what boards, the SEC and NYDFS require of security leaders and what the Uber and SolarWinds records show
Lead the executive layer of a major incident using the Maersk and Change Healthcare cases

lessons.title: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line

blocks.md:
Picture a 300-person software company. Engineers fix vulnerabilities, IT runs the laptops, legal writes the contracts. Someone still has to decide whether next year's money goes to backups or to a new monitoring tool, tell the board which risks are growing, hire the people who do the work, and take the 03:00 call when ransomware hits. That someone is the security leader.

The prerequisite courses taught the parts: risk registers and frameworks (*Risk, governance and compliance for engineers*), the secure SDLC and vulnerability management (*Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management*), and incident process (*Incident response and digital forensics*). This course is the layer above them: strategy, money, people, measurement, crises, regulators and personal liability.

**CISO** stands for *chief information security officer*: the senior executive responsible for an organisation's information security programme. Like CEO or CFO, the "chief ... officer" form marks a member of the top management team. Steve Katz, a banking security executive, recalled being recruited in 1995 after Citicorp was hacked into a job that "was going to be called chief information security officer, the first time that title had ever been used" ([ISC2 tribute, 2023](https://www.isc2.org/insights/2023/12/first-ciso-steve-katz-passes-away)).

Some companies say **CSO** (chief security officer), often covering physical security too. Regulators now define the role. New York's financial regulator, NYDFS (New York State Department of Financial Services), writes in its cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500 (NYCRR: New York Codes, Rules and Regulations): a CISO is "a qualified individual responsible for overseeing and implementing a covered entity's cybersecurity program and enforcing its cybersecurity policy."

The job has four parts:

1. **Direction**: decide what the programme is trying to achieve and in what order (lessons 2 to 4).
2. **Resources**: get money and people, and spend them where they remove the most risk (lessons 5 to 7, 10 and 11).
3. **Visibility**: measure the programme and make risk visible to the people who own it, up to the board (lessons 8 and 9).
4. **Response**: lead the executive side of crises and deal with regulators honestly (lessons 13 to 15).

What the job is not: owning every risk decision. Recall the Three Lines Model: the business owner of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it; the CISO advises, measures and challenges.

**Reporting line** means whom the CISO works for. In a 2025 survey of 662 CISOs by IANS Research and Artico Search (a security research firm and an executive search firm), 64% reported into IT leadership and 36% to business leaders such as the CEO, chief operating officer, general counsel or chief risk officer ([IANS, January 2026](https://www.ians.com/press/2026-report-finds-executive-level-ciso-titles-more-prevalent-than-ever)).

Each line has a trade-off:

- **Under the CIO** (chief information officer): close to the technology, but security competes with IT for the same budget and may have to report weaknesses in the CIO's own systems.
- **Under the CEO**: authority and a seat where trade-offs are made, but more distance from engineering detail.
- **Under the general counsel**: close to legal and regulatory work. Recall that the House report on Equifax quoted the former CIO: security under the Chief Legal Officer was not typical. When Equifax hired Jamil Farshchi as CISO in February 2018, the new CEO told the Senate the CISO reported directly to the CEO.

blocks.title: Three places to put the CISO, and what each one sees

scenes.caption: Most common (64% in the IANS survey): the CISO reports to the CIO. Close to the systems, but every finding about IT systems travels through the person who runs them.
Under the CEO: the CISO sits where budget trade-offs are made. Equifax moved to this line after its 2017 breach.
Under the general counsel: close to regulators and legal advice, but further from engineering. Equifax had this line before the breach.
Whatever the line, a direct channel to the board's audit committee lets bad news arrive unfiltered. The line decides who can filter information, not how good security is.

blocks.md: Misconception: "a higher reporting line means better security". The reporting line decides two things: whether bad news can be filtered before it reaches the people who decide, and whether the CISO is grading their own boss's work. A CISO under the CEO with no budget and no board access can be weaker than one under a CIO with a standing audit-committee slot.

A security leader sets direction, secures resources, makes risk visible to its owners and leads in crises. The reporting line should keep information flowing to the decision makers without a filter or a conflict of interest.

blocks.question: A CISO reports to the CIO. The CIO's infrastructure team owns 40 unpatched internet-facing servers. What is the main governance risk of this reporting line here?
options: The CISO cannot technically scan the servers
The finding about the CIO's own systems may be softened or delayed before it reaches the CEO and board
The CIO is legally barred from fixing servers the CISO has flagged
Reporting to the CIO makes the CISO the owner of the risk
blocks.explain: The issue is a conflict of interest in the information path, not technical access. Risk ownership stays with the business or system owner under the Three Lines Model; a direct audit-committee channel is the usual remedy.

blocks.question: Which of these is NOT part of the CISO's job as this lesson defines it?
options: Deciding on the business owner's behalf to accept a high risk to a revenue system
Building a roadmap and budget for the programme
Reporting the top risks and their trend to the board
Leading the executive side of a major incident
blocks.explain: Risk acceptance belongs to the owner of the system and the delegation of authority (recall the first lesson of the risk course). The CISO advises, measures and challenges; accepting risk quietly on the owner's behalf hides it from the people with budget and authority.

lessons.title: Building a programme from zero: the first 90 days

blocks.md:
You are the first security lead at a 250-person SaaS company. There is no asset inventory, single sign-on (SSO) covers half the applications, backups have never been restored, and a big customer wants a SOC 2 report within nine months.

Two naive starts fail. **Buying tools first** produces alerts nobody owns about assets nobody listed. **Writing forty policies first** produces documents that do not match reality, which an auditor will read as documented failure (recall *Policies people follow*). A programme starts by finding out what exists, what matters and who owns it.

**Days 0 to 30: listen and inventory.**

- Meet every executive and ask what would hurt the business most. This finds the **crown jewels**: the few assets whose loss or compromise would do the most damage (customer data store, payment flow, source code, identity provider).
- Build a first asset and owner list, even a spreadsheet, and the top risks in a register (recall the risk course's register and FAIR estimates).
- Record a current profile against NIST CSF 2.0 (recall: current and target profiles) and every external commitment already made: contracts, audits, regulators, insurance questionnaires.
- Find out who would be called in an incident tonight.

**Days 30 to 60: quick wins.** Pick actions that remove a whole class of risk cheaply and need nothing else first:

- MFA (multi-factor authentication) on email, the identity provider and every admin account.
- A real **restore test** of the most important backup.
- Close public storage buckets and internet-exposed admin panels found in the inventory.
- An incident contact list, an out-of-band channel and, if affordable, a retainer with a response firm (recall *Preparation*).
- A named risk owner for each top risk.

**Days 60 to 90: plan and govern.** Write a one-page strategy (lesson 4), a 12 to 18 month roadmap, a budget ask (lesson 5), a baseline for a handful of metrics (lesson 8) and a monthly forum where owners review risks.

scenes.caption: Weeks 1 to 4: interviews, crown jewels, asset and owner list, risk register, current profile. Nothing is bought yet.
Weeks 5 to 8: quick wins start while the inventory keeps improving. MFA on admins and a restore test need no prior project.
Weeks 9 to 13: strategy, roadmap, budget and metric baseline, built on what the first two months found. Quick wins continue to finish.

blocks.prompt: Your CEO offers to approve one purchase in week 2: a SIEM (security information and event management, a central log search and alerting system) for USD 300k a year, or nothing until day 60. What do you recommend, and why?
blocks.reveal: Usually: not yet. In week 2 you do not know which systems exist, which logs matter or who would answer an alert at night, so the SIEM would ingest whatever is easy and alert nobody useful. Ask instead for small approvals that need no inventory (MFA on admin and email accounts, a restore test, a response retainer) and bring the SIEM decision to the day-90 budget with a logging plan tied to the crown jewels. Saying "not yet" with a date is still an answer.

blocks.md: Do not promise a compliance date (a SOC 2 report, an ISO certificate) before you know the current state. Recall that SOC 2 Type II needs a period of operating evidence: a date picked in week one becomes a commitment you may have to break publicly.

Inventory and owners first, then cheap actions that remove whole classes of risk, then a written strategy and budget built on what you found. Tools come after you know what they will watch and who will respond.

blocks.question: Which first-month action gives the best base for everything after it?
options: Buying an EDR (endpoint detection and response) licence for every laptop
Writing a full policy set from a template
Listing crown-jewel assets with named owners and the top risks in a register
Scheduling an external penetration test
blocks.explain: Every later decision (what to protect first, what to log, whom to call, what to test) depends on knowing the assets and their owners. The other options are useful later but are aimed blind without that list.

blocks.question: Which pair is a good day 30 to 60 quick win?
options: A three-year zero trust architecture programme
A custom detection engineering pipeline
Replacing the firewall vendor
MFA on email, identity provider and admin accounts, and a real restore of the most important backup
blocks.explain: Quick wins are cheap, need no earlier project and remove a whole class of risk: stolen passwords and untested backups. The others are large projects with dependencies that belong on the roadmap.

lessons.title: Maturity models: measuring where you are with C2M2 levels

blocks.md:
After 90 days the board asks: "how mature is our security?" You need a scale that is shared, repeatable and honest. A **maturity model**, in the words of the C2M2 itself, is "a set of characteristics, attributes, indicators, or patterns that represent capability and progression in a particular discipline." It gives a benchmark for where you are and a way to state where you want to be.

**C2M2** is the *Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model* from the US Department of Energy (DOE), developed with the energy industry but usable by any organisation. Version 1.0 appeared in 2012; version 2.1 (June 2022) groups more than 350 practices into 10 **domains**, such as Asset, Change, and Configuration Management (ASSET), Identity and Access Management (ACCESS) and Event and Incident Response, Continuity of Operations (RESPONSE).

Maturity is scored per domain as a **MIL** (maturity indicator level), 0 to 3:

- **MIL0**: practices are not performed.
- **MIL1**: initial practices are performed, but may be ad hoc (depending on one person's initiative rather than a plan).
- **MIL2**: practices are documented and resourced, and more complete.
- **MIL3**: activities are guided by policy, responsibility and authority are assigned, people have the skills, effectiveness is evaluated and tracked, and practices are more advanced still.

Two scoring rules matter. In the DOE self-evaluation tools a practice counts as performed if it is *Fully* or *Largely Implemented* (not *Partially* or *Not Implemented*). And MILs are **cumulative**: "To earn a MIL in a given domain, an organization must perform all practices in that level and in the preceding level."

blocks.caption: Scoring three domains from self-evaluation answers (FI, LI, PI, NI = fully, largely, partially, not implemented). Sample answers are invented; the rules are C2M2's.

blocks.code:
ASSET     MIL1  target MIL2  gap of 1
ACCESS    MIL2  target MIL2  meets target
RESPONSE  MIL0  target MIL3  gap of 3
blocks.caption: Real output. RESPONSE has every MIL2 and MIL3 practice fully implemented, but one partial MIL1 practice holds it at MIL0.

blocks.title: Current level, target level and gap per domain

scenes.caption: Current MILs from the script: ASSET 1, ACCESS 2, RESPONSE 0. The zero is surprising given how advanced the RESPONSE practices are.
Targets chosen by the business: RESPONSE matters most for this company (it runs a 24x7 service), so it gets MIL3; the others MIL2.
Gaps: 1, 0 and 3. The RESPONSE gap of 3 is mostly one missing basic practice; fixing it first lifts the domain straight to MIL3 because the higher practices already exist.

blocks.md:
**Targets, not maximums.** C2M2 says plainly: "Striving to achieve the highest MIL in all domains may not be optimal. Companies should evaluate the costs of achieving a specific MIL versus its potential benefits." It also says the model was designed so that every organisation, whatever its size, should be able to reach MIL1 in all domains. Its recommended cycle: self-evaluate, choose a **target profile** (the desired MIL per domain), analyse gaps, prioritise by business importance and cost, implement, repeat.

Other models you already know play different roles: CSF tiers describe the rigour of risk governance overall, not a level per control (recall the CSF lesson), and OWASP SAMM measures an application security programme (recall the appsec course).

A maturity score measures capability, not outcomes. A domain at MIL3 can still miss an intrusion, and self-evaluations drift upward when the people scoring are the people judged. Ask for evidence for each "Fully Implemented", and pair the maturity view with outcome metrics (lesson 8).

blocks.question: A domain's self-evaluation: all MIL2 and MIL3 practices Fully Implemented; MIL1 practices: three Fully, one Partially Implemented. What MIL does C2M2 assign?
options: MIL0, because MILs are cumulative and one MIL1 practice is not performed
MIL3, because most practices are advanced
MIL2, rounding down
It cannot be scored
blocks.explain: A practice counts only if Fully or Largely Implemented, and every practice at a level and all levels below must be performed. One partial MIL1 practice stops the climb at MIL0, which is why basic gaps deserve attention before advanced work.

blocks.question: A director asks why the target profile is not MIL3 in every domain. Best answer?
options: Because the auditors would object
Because MIL3 everywhere would cost more than the risk reduction it buys in low-impact domains; targets follow business importance, as C2M2 itself recommends
Because MIL3 cannot be reached by any company
Because C2M2 forbids MIL3 outside the energy sector
blocks.explain: C2M2 states that the highest MIL in all domains may not be optimal and that costs should be weighed against benefits. MIL3 is reachable, and the model is not limited to energy.

lessons.title: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies

blocks.md:
A list of gaps is not a strategy. A **strategy**, in the sense the strategy scholar Richard Rumelt sets out in *Good Strategy Bad Strategy* (2011), says three things: what situation you are in (the diagnosis), what you have chosen to do *and not to do* about it, and which coordinated actions follow. A **roadmap** is the actions placed in time with owners.

Tiny example for our SaaS company: *"Diagnosis: our biggest exposures are stolen employee logins and a ransomware event we could not recover from within a week. Choice: for 12 months we put identity and recovery ahead of everything else, and we will not start a data loss prevention (DLP) programme this year. Actions: SSO everywhere, then phishing-resistant MFA; immutable backups, then quarterly restore tests."* The sentence "we will not start" is what makes it a strategy: it tells people what to stop asking for.

A public example of a security strategy with a stated trade-off is Microsoft's **Secure Future Initiative** (SFI), launched in November 2023 and widened in May 2024, after the US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) criticised its security culture (lesson 12). SFI rests on three principles, *secure by design*, *secure by default* and *secure operations*, and six engineering pillars: protect identities and secrets; protect tenants and isolate production systems; protect networks; protect engineering systems; monitor and detect threats; accelerate response and remediation.

The trade-off was explicit. CEO Satya Nadella wrote to employees in May 2024: "If you're faced with the tradeoff between security and another priority, your answer is clear: Do security." ([Microsoft, 3 May 2024](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2024/05/03/prioritizing-security-above-all-else/))

Sequencing follows **dependencies**: an item can start only when the things it needs are finished. Common ones:

- An asset inventory before vulnerability SLAs (you cannot measure fix times for assets you cannot list).
- SSO before phishing-resistant MFA (enforce strong login once, at the identity provider, rather than in every app).
- Central logging before detections and an on-call rota.
- Immutable backups before restore tests of them.

The team's **capacity** limits how many workstreams run at once. The script below places each initiative in the first quarter where its dependencies are done and a workstream is free.

blocks.code:
# Place initiatives into quarters. Each one occupies one workstream for its
# duration, and can start only after all its dependencies have finished.
items = {  # name: (quarters, dependencies)
    "asset inventory":      (1, []),
    "SSO for all apps":     (2, []),
    "immutable backups":    (1, []),
    "phish-resistant MFA":  (1, ["SSO for all apps"]),
    "vuln mgmt SLAs":       (1, ["asset inventory"]),
    "central logging":      (1, ["asset inventory"]),
    "detections + on-call": (2, ["central logging"]),
    "restore test":         (1, ["immutable backups"]),
}
STREAMS = 3                  # parallel workstreams the team can run
start, end = {}, {}
q = 0
while len(end) < len(items):
    q += 1
    busy = sum(1 for n in start if start[n] <= q <= end[n])
    for name, (dur, deps) in items.items():
        ready = all(d in end and end[d] < q for d in deps)
        if name not in start and ready and busy < STREAMS:
            start[name], end[name] = q, q + dur - 1
            busy += 1

for q in range(1, max(end.values()) + 1):
    running = [n for n in start if start[n] <= q <= end[n]]
    print(f"Q{q}: {', '.join(running)}")
blocks.caption: A dependency- and capacity-aware roadmap. Durations, dependencies and three parallel workstreams are invented for the example.

blocks.code:
Q1: asset inventory, SSO for all apps, immutable backups
Q2: SSO for all apps, vuln mgmt SLAs, central logging
Q3: phish-resistant MFA, detections + on-call, restore test
Q4: detections + on-call
blocks.caption: Real output. Detections cannot start until central logging is done (Q2), and logging waits for the inventory (Q1).

blocks.title: The roadmap from the script, by workstream

scenes.caption: Q1: three items with no dependencies fill the three workstreams. SSO takes two quarters.
Q2: the inventory is done, so vulnerability SLAs and central logging can start. SSO still occupies its workstream.
Q3 and Q4: MFA follows SSO, detections follow logging (two quarters), the restore test follows backups. Everything ends in Q4.

blocks.md: A strategy is a diagnosis, a choice (including what you will not do) and coordinated actions. A roadmap places those actions by dependency and capacity, with an owner and a measurable outcome for each item. Re-plan it every quarter and show the board what is unfunded.

blocks.question: In the script's roadmap, what decides that 'detections + on-call' cannot start before Q3?
options: Detections are always scheduled last
Its duration is two quarters
The team has only two workstreams
It depends on central logging, which depends on the asset inventory, so the earliest start is Q3
blocks.explain: The chain inventory (Q1) then logging (Q2) then detections (Q3 and Q4) fixes the earliest start. Duration affects when it ends, not when it can begin; the team has three workstreams.

blocks.question: Which statement is a strategy rather than a wish?
options: We will be world-class in security
We will improve our posture across all areas this year
For 12 months identity and recovery come first; we will not start a DLP programme this year
Security is everyone's responsibility
blocks.explain: Only that option contains a diagnosis-driven choice and an explicit thing not to do, which lets people decide what to stop asking for. The others cannot guide a single resource decision.

lessons.title: Budgets: what security costs and how to ask for money

blocks.md:
The CFO asks: "how much should security cost us?" There are three honest inputs: what similar organisations spend (benchmarks), what your risks justify (recall FAIR and the Gordon-Loeb model from the risk course: spending has diminishing returns), and what you are already obliged to pay for (audits, contracts, regulation). A budget built from only one of them is easy to attack.

**Benchmarks, with their caveats.** IANS Research and Artico Search survey CISOs every year. Their 2025 report (587 CISOs) found average budget growth of 4%, down from 8% in 2024, and security spending falling from 11.9% to 10.9% of IT spend ([IANS, August 2025](https://www.ians.com/press/ians-research-and-artico-search-release-security-budget-benchmark-report)). The 2026 report (more than 500 security executives) found average growth of 5%, and budgets of about USD 1 million a year at companies with revenue up to USD 100 million against more than USD 30 million above USD 10 billion ([Cybersecurity Dive, September 2026](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/ai-leading-driver-cybersecurity-spending/830418/)).

Treat these numbers carefully:

- They are **self-reported surveys** of CISOs who chose to answer, run by a research firm and a recruiting firm, not audited accounts.
- **Averages hide spread**: a few large increases lift the average while many budgets stay flat.
- **Definitions differ**: one company counts identity, backup or fraud teams as security, another does not.

**Breach-cost figures** need the same care. IBM's *Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026*, researched by the Ponemon Institute (a privacy and security research firm), puts the global average cost of a breach at USD 4.99 million, 12% more than a year earlier ([IBM](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach)). It is sponsored by a security vendor, built from organisations that had a breach and agreed to take part, and its averages include estimated items such as lost business. It is context, not your expected loss; your own FAIR estimate is the number to defend.

A budget has three parts:

- **People**: salaries times a **loaded cost** factor (benefits, payroll tax, equipment, training). For most security teams this is the largest line.
- **Run**: what it costs to keep today's controls working: licences, managed services, audits, penetration tests. Run costs recur every year.
- **Change**: projects that build new capability (an SSO migration, backup isolation). They end, but often leave new run costs behind.

Finance teams may also split spending into **OPEX** (operating expenditure, expensed in the year it is spent) and **CAPEX** (capital expenditure on assets that are depreciated over several years); ask your finance partner which items they treat as which.

blocks.code:
# A made-up 1,200-person company. All figures USD thousands per year.
EMPLOYEES, IT_BUDGET = 1200, 38000
LOADED = 1.3     # salary x 1.3 for benefits, tax, equipment (assumed)

people = {"CISO": (1, 330), "GRC": (2, 150), "SecOps": (4, 160),
          "AppSec": (3, 175), "Cloud/IAM": (2, 180)}  # (headcount, salary)
run = {"EDR": 210, "SIEM + storage": 380, "email security": 70,
       "IdP/MFA": 160, "MDR night cover": 300, "pentests": 120,
       "audit (SOC 2)": 90}
change = {"SSO migration": 250, "backup isolation": 200}

staff = sum(n * s * LOADED for n, s in people.values())
lines = {"people": staff, "run: tools+services": sum(run.values()),
         "change: projects": sum(change.values())}
total = sum(lines.values())
for k, v in lines.items():
    print(f"{k:<22} {v:>7.0f}k  {v / total:>4.0%}")
print(f"{'total':<22} {total:>7.0f}k")
print(f"share of IT budget:    {total / IT_BUDGET:.1%}")
print(f"per employee:          USD {total * 1000 / EMPLOYEES:,.0f}")

blocks.md:
How to ask for money so that a CFO can say yes:

- Tie every line to one of three reasons: **risk removed** (expected loss reduced, lesson 6), an **obligation** (contract, regulation, audit), or **run cost** of something already decided.
- Offer **options**, not a single number: do nothing (and the risk that remains, with its owner), minimum, recommended.
- Show **what you will stop paying for** (lesson 7) and what change projects will add to next year's run cost.
- Recall Gordon-Loeb: the first dollars on a large exposure remove the most loss; say where you are on that curve.

Weak argument: "the average breach costs USD 4.99 million, so give us 1 million." The average is not your loss, the board knows it, and the request names no risk and no result. Strong argument: "this USD 250k removes an estimated 700k of expected annual loss from ransomware on our order system, according to our FAIR model with these ranges."

blocks.question: Which budget justification is the most defensible to a CFO?
options: This line removes an estimated USD 700k of expected annual loss from a named risk; this one is required by a customer contract; this one is the run cost of last year's SSO project
Our spend is below the IANS average of 10.9% of IT, so we should raise it to the average
Average breach costs rose 12% this year, so security must grow 12%
Peer companies have bigger teams
blocks.explain: Each line has a reason the CFO can check: risk removed, an obligation, or an existing commitment. Benchmarks and industry averages describe other organisations and cannot tell you whether a specific line is worth it.

blocks.question: The 2025 IANS figure of 10.9% of IT spend is best used as...
options: A target every company should hit
A rough sense check from a self-reported survey, with definitions that vary between companies
A regulatory minimum
Proof that budgets are falling everywhere
blocks.explain: It is a self-reported average from responding CISOs. It can flag a budget far outside the usual range, but it is not a target, a rule, or a statement about every company.

lessons.title: Prioritising a portfolio: expected loss removed per dollar

blocks.md:
You have USD 900k and six good ideas. Funding all of them would cost 1.81 million. Something has to give, and the question is how to choose.

Recall from the risk course: **ALE** (annualised loss expectancy) is the expected loss per year from a risk, and a FAIR analysis gives it with ranges. For each option, the **loss removed** is the ALE before minus the ALE after. That turns "which idea is best?" into a comparison of numbers you can argue about openly.

Three ways people actually choose:

1. **Headline-driven**: fund what last month's news made people afraid of.
2. **Largest benefit first**: fund the option that removes the most loss, then the next, until the money runs out.
3. **Benefit per dollar**: rank by loss removed divided by cost, then fund in that order.

The third is the classic greedy answer to what computer science calls the **knapsack problem** (choose items with values and weights to maximise value within a weight limit). Greedy is not always optimal, so with few options it is worth checking every combination.

blocks.code:
from itertools import combinations

# name: (cost per year, expected annual loss removed), USD thousands.
# Loss removed = ALE before minus ALE after, from the risk register.
options = {
    "EDR on servers":           (400, 520),
    "phish-resistant MFA":      (150, 610),
    "immutable backups":        (250, 700),
    "DLP suite":                (500, 300),
    "secrets scanning in CI":   (60, 180),
    "24x7 MDR service":         (450, 650),
}
BUDGET = 900

def value(names):
    return sum(options[n][1] for n in names)

def cost(names):
    return sum(options[n][0] for n in names)

# 1. fund what last month's headlines made people afraid of
by_fear = ["DLP suite", "EDR on servers", "24x7 MDR service"]
# 2. fund the biggest benefit first until money runs out
by_size = sorted(options, key=lambda n: -options[n][1])
# 3. fund by loss removed per dollar spent
by_ratio = sorted(options, key=lambda n: -options[n][1] / options[n][0])
for label, order in [("headline-driven", by_fear),
                     ("largest benefit first", by_size),
                     ("benefit per dollar", by_ratio)]:
    chosen = []
    for n in order:
        if cost(chosen) + options[n][0] <= BUDGET:
            chosen.append(n)
    print(f"{label:<22} spend {cost(chosen)}k removes {value(chosen)}k")

# 4. check every combination (64 subsets)
best = max((c for r in range(len(options) + 1)
            for c in combinations(options, r) if cost(c) <= BUDGET),
           key=value)
print(f"{'best possible':<22} spend {cost(best)}k removes {value(best)}k")
print("  ", ", ".join(best))

largest benefit first  spend 850k removes 1960k
benefit per dollar     spend 860k removes 2010k
best possible          spend 860k removes 2010k

blocks.title: Same budget, four ways to choose (USD thousands)

scenes.caption: Expected loss removed per year. Headline-driven funding (DLP suite plus EDR) removes 820k; the others remove 1,960k to 2,010k.
Money spent: 900k, 850k, 860k, 860k. The worst choice spends the most. Spending everything is not the goal; removing loss is.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the MFA estimate was too optimistic and it really removes 305k, not 610k. Does the funded set change?
blocks.reveal: No. Re-running the script with 305k gives the same four options (EDR on servers, phishing-resistant MFA, immutable backups, secrets scanning), now removing 1,705k instead of 2,010k; benefit per dollar still matches the best combination. A decision that survives a halving of its most uncertain input is **robust**, which is worth telling the board. When a decision flips with small changes in an estimate, spend effort on improving that estimate before committing.

blocks.md:
Real portfolios add constraints the script ignores:

- **Obligations** (a contractual audit, a legal requirement) are funded first, whatever their ratio.
- **Dependencies** (lesson 4) mean some high-ratio items cannot start until a low-ratio foundation is done.
- **Uncertainty**: use ranges and Monte Carlo (recall the risk course) instead of single numbers.

Then **say no in writing**. Every unfunded risk goes back to its owner with the estimate, the option you could not fund, and a request to accept it with an expiry date (recall risk treatment and exceptions). A clear "not funded" list protects the organisation and you: the decision is visible and owned.

Rank by expected loss removed per dollar, check combinations when options are few, fund obligations and foundations first, test whether the decision survives changes to the shakiest estimate, and hand every unfunded risk back to its owner in writing.

blocks.question: Why does the 'largest benefit first' rule remove less loss than 'benefit per dollar' in the script?
options: It always picks the cheapest option first
It cannot handle more than four options
It ignores costs, so an expensive option (the 450k MDR service) uses budget that could fund cheaper options with more total benefit
It double counts the backup option
blocks.explain: Picking by size alone spends 450k on the MDR service, which then blocks EDR. Dividing by cost favours the options that remove the most loss for each dollar, here leaving room for EDR.

blocks.question: An option removes little expected loss per dollar but is required by a signed customer contract. What should happen?
options: Fund it as an obligation, and record why it sits outside the ranking
Drop it; ratios decide everything
Hide it in another line
Ask the customer to remove the clause before deciding
blocks.explain: Obligations are funded regardless of ratio, and the reason is recorded so the portfolio stays explainable. The ranking applies to discretionary spending.

lessons.title: Vendors and tools: buy, build, consolidate and plan the exit

blocks.md:
Security teams accumulate tools: one bought after an incident, one that came with a bundle, one a previous leader liked. Each costs licences, people's time and an integration to maintain. **Tool rationalisation** means checking which capabilities you need, which tool provides each one, and retiring tools that add nothing unique.

Tiny example: five tools cost 1,110k a year. The script asks two questions per tool: what would we lose if it went, and can we remove the most expensive tools one by one without losing any capability?

blocks.code:
# Which tool covers which capability, and what each costs (USD k/year).
tools = {
    "EDR A":        (300, {"endpoint detect", "host isolation", "threat intel"}),
    "SIEM B":       (420, {"log search", "detection rules", "threat intel"}),
    "Email gw C":   (90,  {"phish filter", "url rewrite"}),
    "XDR add-on D": (180, {"endpoint detect", "detection rules", "log search"}),
    "Intel feed E": (120, {"threat intel"}),
}
needed = set().union(*(caps for _, caps in tools.values()))

for name, (cost, caps) in tools.items():
    others = set().union(*(c for n, (_, c) in tools.items() if n != name))
    unique = caps - others          # what we lose if this tool goes
    print(f"{name:<13} {cost:>4}k  unique: {sorted(unique) or 'none'}")

# Remove tools that add nothing unique, one at a time, re-checking each time
keep = dict(tools)
for name in sorted(tools, key=lambda n: -tools[n][0]):
    rest = set().union(*(c for n, (_, c) in keep.items() if n != name))
    if rest >= needed:
        del keep[name]
        print(f"retire {name}: saves {tools[name][0]}k, coverage intact")
print("keep:", ", ".join(keep), f"total {sum(c for c, _ in keep.values())}k")
blocks.caption: Tools, their capabilities and costs are invented. XDR (extended detection and response) joins endpoint, email, identity and cloud signals in one platform. The retirement loop tries the most expensive tool first and re-checks coverage after each removal.

blocks.code:

SIEM B         420k  unique: none
Email gw C      90k  unique: ['phish filter', 'url rewrite']
XDR add-on D   180k  unique: none
Intel feed E   120k  unique: none
